articles.title: This version
articles.summary: What this version of the course covers, what it leaves out on purpose, and what a later one adds

articles.title: About this wiki
articles.summary: What this course is, who it is written by, and how it differs from the official docs.

articles.title: Changelog
articles.summary: What changed in each version before this one, kept so a returning reader can find the delta

articles.title: How to read this
articles.summary: How to move around this wiki — the keys, the mouse, and where to start.

articles.title: The companion agent
articles.summary: A second way into the course — an agent that has read every page here and answers from it, citing its source

articles.title: What a terminal is
articles.summary: The black window is an app that runs other apps, and it is pretending to be furniture.

articles.title: GUI and TUI
articles.summary: An app made of text and driven by the keyboard, which is what everything was before it was made of pictures.

articles.title: What CLI, command line and prompt mean
articles.summary: Four words for one window, and what each one meant before they collapsed into each other

articles.title: The terminals people use
articles.summary: The terminal on your Mac is not the only one, and the ones people actually reach for differ on five things

articles.title: Your terminal is Ghostty
articles.summary: The terminal you were given, what it does better than the one your Mac came with, and the four keys worth knowing.

articles.title: What was set up for you
articles.summary: Someone else chose your colours and your font before you ever opened Ghostty, and none of it is permanent

articles.title: What tmux is
articles.summary: A program that keeps a terminal session running even after the window looking at it is gone

articles.title: What it is for
articles.summary: Insurance for a long job, a session you can hand to someone else, and several processes on one screen

articles.title: The prefix key
articles.summary: A chord, not a single key, decides whether a keystroke reaches tmux or the program running inside it

articles.title: Sessions
articles.summary: Every tmux command works on a session, and an unnamed one is a number you will forget by the third matter

articles.title: Windows and panes
articles.summary: A window takes the whole screen and a pane shares it, both living and dying with the session underneath them

articles.title: Detaching and reattaching
articles.summary: Leaving a session on purpose and finding it again are each one command, and neither one is closing the window

articles.title: The config file
articles.summary: Every persistent tweak to tmux lives in one file, read once at startup and reloaded on command rather than by restarting

articles.title: Copy mode
articles.summary: Scrollback tmux keeps for itself, and the only way text inside a pane gets out of it

articles.title: The status bar
articles.summary: The one line on screen tmux never lets go blank, and what it is telling you by default

articles.title: What a shell is
articles.summary: The program that greets you when a terminal opens, and what sits underneath it.

articles.title: Why the shell is powerful
articles.summary: Clicking does one thing at a time; a typed command does a thousand, from anywhere.

articles.title: The shells there are
articles.summary: One family of programs, mostly interchangeable, plus a Boss's opinion of the one that is not

articles.title: Your shell is zsh
articles.summary: Which one you actually have, why Apple chose it, and the standard that makes it worth learning once

articles.title: Moving around
articles.summary: Paths, the four commands you need daily, and the fastest way from one folder to a neighbour rather than a stranger

articles.title: zoxide
articles.summary: cd remembers nothing between commands; zoxide remembers every folder you have visited and ranks them for you

articles.title: Permanent variables
articles.summary: A variable typed at the prompt dies with the terminal; the same line in ~/.zshrc survives every one you open after

articles.title: Globbing
articles.summary: A pattern stands for many filenames at once, and zsh expands it before the command you typed ever sees it

articles.title: grep
articles.summary: A glob finds files by name; grep finds them by what is written inside, line by line

articles.title: ripgrep
articles.summary: The same search as grep, defaulting to recursive, skipping what a .gitignore already excludes, fast enough not to notice

articles.title: fzf
articles.summary: rg narrows a search before you look; fzf hands you the list and narrows it live as you type against it

articles.title: Your prompt
articles.summary: The text before the cursor is a status display, and it can say whatever is useful to you.

articles.title: Powerline themes
articles.summary: A prompt built from coloured blocks called segments, each showing a single fact about where you are, and why the seams between them need a special font

articles.title: Starship
articles.summary: The program that draws your prompt from one readable file, with the branch and the duration already switched on before you touch it

articles.title: Every app is a wrapper
articles.summary: What you pay for is rarely the code itself — it is the installer, the window and the logo wrapped around it

articles.title: Packages
articles.summary: Every app is a bundle of code, most of that code is free, and the shell is how you reach it

articles.title: Package managers
articles.summary: The one program that finds a package, checks it is genuine, fetches everything it needs, and keeps the lot working

articles.title: What Homebrew is
articles.summary: The package manager macOS does not come with, and the one nearly every set of instructions online quietly assumes you have

articles.title: Formulae and casks
articles.summary: One kind of Homebrew install gives you a command; the other gives you a whole app with a window

articles.title: Checking and updating
articles.summary: One command a week finds everything out of date and brings it current, instead of fifteen separate update dialogs

articles.title: What a programming language is
articles.summary: A shell drives a machine that already exists; a programming language builds the machine it drives

articles.title: Why plain text wins
articles.summary: A machine can read a plain file without being told how, and almost everything in this course rests on that one fact

articles.title: The formats you will meet
articles.summary: A format is the shape plain text gets cut into, and some shapes forgive a typo while others do not

articles.title: IDEs
articles.summary: A single program built to hold every step of writing software at once, which is not the shape of your day

articles.title: Editors in the terminal
articles.summary: Nano and micro behave the way you already expect; vim, neovim and helix trade discoverability for speed you do not need

articles.title: What Linux is
articles.summary: A kernel, not an operating system — and the distributions that build one around it.

articles.title: The world runs on Linux
articles.summary: Under three percent of desktops and nearly all of everything else — including the machine answering you right now

articles.title: Why it is better
articles.summary: Faster, safer by construction, and honest about what it lacks — before the article that makes the real case.

articles.title: You are the system
articles.summary: Every layer of a Linux machine is a choice you make — and Claude Code is what makes making that choice practical.

articles.title: What an LLM is
articles.summary: A model is a mathematical function that guesses the next word, and that turns out to be enough and not enough

articles.title: What makes one model different from another
articles.summary: Size, architecture and speciality are the three axes, and only one of them is the number everyone quotes

articles.title: The models there are
articles.summary: Cloud models you reach over the internet, open-weight models you can download, and why the second kind is harder than it sounds

articles.title: What a model consumes
articles.summary: Billions of numbers held where they can be multiplied at once, and free is not the same as available to you

articles.title: What a harness is
articles.summary: The model is the brain; a harness is the body that gives it hands

articles.title: The harnesses there are
articles.summary: Claude Code is one harness among a growing field of them, sorted by where they live

articles.title: What a harness consumes
articles.summary: A harness wants almost nothing from your machine, until you ask it to run many of itself at once

articles.title: Renting a computer
articles.summary: When your own machine is not enough, you rent someone else's by the hour rather than buy one

articles.title: What you do with a box
articles.summary: Install what the job needs, run it, and bring home only the result

articles.title: The models
articles.summary: Four Claude models exist, and choosing between them is a trade-off between speed and depth, not a favourite

articles.title: The harnesses
articles.summary: Three ways to reach Claude — a website, a sandboxed website, and a terminal program on your own machine

articles.title: The plans
articles.summary: Four tiers, and the saving from one to the next is a multiple, not a step

articles.title: Why Claude Code
articles.summary: The model lives in a data centre and the harness lives on your Mac, and that split is what this article is really about

articles.title: What it can do that the others cannot
articles.summary: Standing inside your own machine is not only safer, it is more capable — real software and real hardware, not a fixed slice of someone else's

articles.title: Installing
articles.summary: It is already on your Mac — how to check, how to sign in, and how to put it on the next machine.

articles.title: Launching Claude Code
articles.summary: Type claude and press enter — and understand the one thing that changes what happens next.

articles.title: The .claude directory
articles.summary: The harness lives in an ordinary hidden folder called .claude, not on a server.

articles.title: Inside .claude
articles.summary: A tour of what lives inside .claude — more than you need today, so the names are not strange later.

articles.title: More .claude directories
articles.summary: You can have as many as you like, one per folder, and each one makes that folder a project.

articles.title: What a session sees
articles.summary: Claude walks up from the folder you launched in, collecting every .claude on the way.

articles.title: Location matters
articles.summary: More is worse — so split what you build across folders and launch from the right one.

articles.title: The CLAUDE.md file
articles.summary: Claude collects every CLAUDE.md walking up at startup, then reads one again the moment it reaches that folder

articles.title: CLAUDE.md tips
articles.summary: Keep it short, put the summary at the top and the checklist at the bottom, and send anything conditional to a rule instead

articles.title: Rules
articles.summary: A rule is a single instruction kept in its own file, invisible to every session until a CLAUDE.md names it

articles.title: Rules tips
articles.summary: Import a rule only where it always applies, leave the rest unimported, and use two everyday examples to decide which is which

articles.title: What an agent is
articles.summary: Every separate conversation is a separate agent, and it knows nothing about the others.

articles.title: Context
articles.summary: Every agent has a fixed amount of brainspace, and everything it touches fills a little of it.

articles.title: Context rot
articles.summary: As the window fills the agent gets worse at everything, and it never tells you.

articles.title: Managing context
articles.summary: The three resets — compact, clear, exit — and how to pick between them.

articles.title: ccstatusline
articles.summary: A third-party status line that puts the figures Context rot and Managing context asked you to watch on the line under the prompt

articles.title: Changing permission modes
articles.summary: Shift-Tab moves a running session between how closely it checks with you before acting, and a setting moves the one it opens in

articles.title: The permission modes there are
articles.summary: Five settled points on one dial, from asking about everything to reading only and asking about nothing

articles.title: The boss recommends: auto mode
articles.summary: His own default is auto mode, taught once what counts as sensitive and left alone after that

articles.title: The boss recommends: plan mode
articles.summary: A mode built for code that turns out to be just as useful once several agents are the ones being coordinated

articles.title: Prompt dos and donts
articles.summary: A quality target gives an agent nothing to check its own work against; an objective does.

articles.title: Prompt engineering
articles.summary: Three pieces, always in the same order — context, objectives, traps — and a prompt with all three rarely needs a second try.

articles.title: Long prompts
articles.summary: Context, objectives and traps written out in full outgrow the chat box, so there is a keystroke for stepping outside it.

articles.title: Shorthands and key words
articles.summary: A word set once in settings.json means the same thing in every prompt after it, the way a variable means the same thing in every line of a script.

articles.title: The advisor tool
articles.summary: A second model reads the whole transcript and says whether the first one is about to get it wrong, at a cost that is not always worth paying.

articles.title: The default agent
articles.summary: Every plain `claude` gives you the same type of agent — the default one, which has no definition behind it.

articles.title: Custom agents
articles.summary: A custom agent is one file in a `.claude/agents/` folder, launched with `claude --agent`.

articles.title: The definition file
articles.summary: Two parts — frontmatter for the settings, body for the instructions — and most documented settings are noise.

articles.title: The fields that matter
articles.summary: Party Trick #3 — six frontmatter fields do real work, and the rest is decoration.

articles.title: Output styles
articles.summary: An output style changes the register of the whole session, not any single agent's tools or model

articles.title: Building one
articles.summary: Ask the custom-agents skill and answer four questions — including which model does which kind of work.

articles.title: Start with never
articles.summary: Most jobs do not need a skill — try the agents first, and build one only when the same instructions keep coming out of your mouth.

articles.title: What a skill is
articles.summary: A folder holding a SKILL.md and its supporting files — think of it as a custom, much longer prompt you only write once.

articles.title: The frontmatter
articles.summary: Four fields do real work in a SKILL.md — name, description, effort, and user-invocable, which is always true.

articles.title: The body
articles.summary: Where the instructions go — and why you will not be writing them yourself.

articles.title: Supporting files
articles.summary: A skill is a folder, so it can carry templates, checklists and scripts — read only when the instructions point at them.

articles.title: How to build one
articles.summary: Claude writes the skill, but you still have to say what goes in it — and there is an efficient way to say it.

articles.title: Start with examples
articles.summary: Party Trick #4 — build a skill from your own worked examples, and give it the inputs as well as the outputs.

articles.title: Iterate with corrections
articles.summary: Narrow skills work first time; broad ones you patch — say what went wrong and show it the other correct answer.

articles.title: Building your first skill
articles.summary: Ask the custom-skills skill and answer five questions — the important one being how hard it should think.

articles.title: How skills work
articles.summary: Writing a good skill is the easy part — getting it to fire when it should, and only then, is the hard part.

articles.title: Always invoke manually
articles.summary: Party Trick #5 — type a slash, pick the skill off the list, and it fires every time.

articles.title: Reading your own prompt
articles.summary: The picker tells you a skill is missing after you have already started — the directory segment in your prompt can tell you before

articles.title: What a subagent is
articles.summary: Your main agent can open conversations underneath your own, hand out instructions, and take the finished work back.

articles.title: Chain engineering
articles.summary: Party Trick #6 — stack agents and their skills without limit, and Claude stops doing tasks and starts taking on projects.

articles.title: Out of the box
articles.summary: Your default agent already spawns subagents — ask it to, or enter plan mode and watch it propose them itself.

articles.title: Designing a chain
articles.summary: Three shapes, from generic agents on different models to custom agents each running their own skill — and one rule about not mixing.

articles.title: The door
articles.summary: One skill you type a slash into whose only job is to spawn the chain, with every worker skill fired by a slash command on line one of its spawn prompt.

articles.title: Step one — the project
articles.summary: Make a folder of its own, and ask Claude for three documents to point the chain at.

articles.title: Step two — the workers
articles.summary: Four builds — two agents and two skills — each one a short interview you have already been walked through.

articles.title: Step three — the door
articles.summary: One more skill, and this one does no work — it spawns the four you already built.

articles.title: Step four — run it
articles.summary: One line, five parts, and a chronology out the other end — with a way to tell whether it is right.

articles.title: Step five — watch it
articles.summary: Read a chain while it runs, fix it in the skill that got it wrong, and the chain is yours.

articles.title: What a workflow is
articles.summary: The same idea as a chain with the driving seat taken out — a script calls every agent instead of one you can talk to

articles.title: What they buy and what they cost
articles.summary: A fixed script cannot forget a step, and that guarantee is paid for in agents that take longer to start and cost more to run

articles.title: When to use one
articles.summary: One pipeline, run ten times over or ten times at once, with none of the sessions and none of the management

articles.title: Sessions that survive
articles.summary: Start the workflow inside a named tmux session, detach, and it keeps running with the lid shut

articles.title: How to build a workflow
articles.summary: Ask the main agent for a workflow the same way you ask for a chain, on the effort level built for it

articles.title: Making it thinner
articles.summary: What Claude hands back first is oversized on purpose — push back on the count, the models, and whether an LLM was ever needed

articles.title: What git is
articles.summary: Git is not only for code, and the Boss treats it as the one indispensable safeguard against an agent's own trigger-happy edits

articles.title: How git works
articles.summary: Files are tracked or ignored, changes are staged before they are committed, and a remote can be a server or a drive as easily as GitHub

articles.title: GitHub
articles.summary: GitHub hosts the remote git already knows how to talk to, and its real value to you is the working software sitting in other people's repositories

articles.title: Jujutsu
articles.summary: Jujutsu reads the same history as git but removes the staging step and the state where work can go missing, saving on its own as you go

articles.title: Git and the harness
articles.summary: A folder becomes a repository and a coding harness gets three things it did not have before — a history to undo into, room for several agents on one file, and drafts it can merge into one

articles.title: Worktrees
articles.summary: A worktree gives one repository several working folders at once, so agents that need to touch the same project simultaneously never collide

articles.title: Forking
articles.summary: A forked subagent starts from the conversation you are already in rather than an empty one, which is worth it for a second opinion, not for splitting a job up

articles.title: What a hook is
articles.summary: A script that fires by itself on a trigger, which is the only part of Claude Code that is not a request

articles.title: The triggers
articles.summary: The named moments a hook can attach to, and knowing the list is what tells you a hook is even possible

articles.title: Scoping a hook
articles.summary: A hook obeys the same placement rule as everything else, plus one further axis — which agent, or which tool

articles.title: SessionStart and SubagentStart
articles.summary: A SessionStart hook briefs an agent before it reads a word, and a SubagentStart hook does the same the instant a subagent spawns

articles.title: PreToolUse
articles.summary: A PreToolUse hook can see a tool call coming and refuse it outright, before a single line changes

articles.title: PostToolUse and FileChanged
articles.summary: PostToolUse fires once Claude's own tool call is done, and FileChanged fires when a file changes for any reason at all, including one Claude was never told about

articles.title: SessionEnd and SubagentStop
articles.summary: SessionEnd closes out a whole conversation and SubagentStop checks a single subagent's work, both asking whether what was supposed to happen actually did

articles.title: CwdChanged and DirectoryAdded
articles.summary: CwdChanged fires when an agent's working directory moves and DirectoryAdded fires when a new one enters its reach, both forcing a read that would otherwise wait on chance

articles.title: WorktreeCreate and WorktreeRemove
articles.summary: the closing pair of triggers, firing when a second working copy of a repository appears or disappears beside the first

articles.title: What a plugin is
articles.summary: A plugin is a portable .claude directory, built once and installed anywhere rather than written into one project

articles.title: When to make one
articles.summary: Four cases where a suite belongs outside any one project, and the one where a plugin earns its keep every single day

articles.title: What is inside one
articles.summary: The same folders as .claude, plus one extra folder that is what actually turns an ordinary directory into a plugin

articles.title: How a plugin works
articles.summary: A manifest names it, a marketplace lists it, and installing it is a choice of scope you already know how to make

articles.title: Building one
articles.summary: You do not hand-write a manifest or a marketplace listing; you tell Claude what to bundle and it writes both

articles.title: Exercises
articles.summary: Take something you already built, turn it into a plugin, and prove it by installing it somewhere else

articles.title: What a headless session is
articles.summary: Type claude -p and a prompt on the same line, and Claude Code answers once and hands the shell straight back

articles.title: When to use one
articles.summary: Not for working something out — for running work you have already worked out, three shapes of it

articles.title: Piping
articles.summary: The one shell operator Moving around left out on purpose, and the reason a headless session needed it first

articles.title: Watching
articles.summary: A headless session prints once and stops talking, which is not the same as nothing happening in between

articles.title: Builtin agents
articles.summary: Turn off the agents Claude Code dispatches on its own initiative and let a custom agent built for the job stand in their place

articles.title: Background sessions and agent view
articles.summary: What a background session and agent view actually cost, and the one setting that turns off both together

articles.title: Subagents spawning subagents
articles.summary: A structural fix for a feature the Boss says to switch off entirely, with the bug that made him say it

articles.title: Agent teams
articles.summary: Teammates that message each other while they work and still get switched off before anything with a deadline attached
